abstract: Periodontitis involves an imbalanced immune microenvironment, characterized by an increased Th17/Treg ratio and iron overload-associated ferroptosis, which hinder alveolar bone repair. Although aggregate-derived extracellular vesicles (EVs) from mesenchymal stem cells have been shown to modulate the Th17/Treg balance in periodontal tissues and to be more potent than single-cell-derived EVs in regulating CD4⁺ T cell differentiation, the underlying mechanisms remain largely unclear. To address this, we compared the protein cargo of EVs from stem cells from human exfoliated deciduous teeth and umbilical cord mesenchymal stem cells cultured as aggregates or single cells. Our results suggest that aggregate culture may upregulate ferritin heavy chain 1 (FTH1) in EVs derived from MSCs of both ectodermal and mesodermal origins. FTH1 promoted collagen synthesis within aggregates and increased the yield of aggregate-derived EVs. Under inflammatory conditions, EV-delivered FTH1 maintained glutathione peroxidase 4 levels in T cells and reduced lipid peroxidation, suppressing ferroptosis and rebalancing Th17/Treg differentiation. Furthermore, in a rat periodontitis model, FTH1 was required for EVs to restore the Th17/Treg balance and promote alveolar bone repair. These findings suggest that the EV-FTH1-ferroptosis pathway could serve as a novel target for periodontal immunotherapy.
